## TCGPMD.
<note>original: "TCGPMD." These initials likely represent the owner of the book. In the 17th century, it was common for wealthy bibliophiles to have their initials and coat of arms stamped on the cover, a practice known as a <term>supralibros</term> (literally "upon the book").</note>

[The front cover of this 17th-century volume is crafted from brown leather, featuring intricate designs created through blind-stamping—a process where decorative tools are pressed into the leather without the use of gold leaf. At the center is a large, elegant oval containing a heraldic coat of arms.]

[The shield within the oval is divided into four quarters: the first and fourth sections feature three fleurs-de-lis <term>fleur-de-lis: a stylized lily flower often used in heraldry to signify royalty or excellence</term>, while the second and third sections show a chequy <term>chequy: a checkered pattern of alternating colors</term> design. The shield is crowned by a ceremonial helmet with decorative scrolling greenery. At the very top of the helmet sits a crest featuring a six-pointed star held between two outspread wings.]

[The entire cover is framed by a rectangular border of fine lines, with floral stamps decorating the corners and the middle of each side.]

*to reduce them to any index. For Mizaldus* <note>Antoine Mizauld (1510–1578), a French physician and astrologer whose "Books of Secrets" were immensely popular for their mix of natural philosophy and practical recipes.</note> *prefixed only the summaries of individual* **secrets** <term>arcanorum <gloss>hidden mysteries or specialized pieces of knowledge</gloss></term> *to each* **Century** <note>A "Century" is a grouping of 100 items, a common way to organize collections of aphorisms or natural observations during the Renaissance.</note> *according to the order of their numbers, not by their topics or alphabetically.*
*For although those accurate indices we use today relieve many people of much labor and even greatly assist the learned, nevertheless, because this provides an excuse for most never to read through the books themselves—or rather, to touch upon them only lightly, placing their memory in the indexes rather than the books—it truly would have been nothing other, to compile any further indexes, than to cater to the lazy. It would have been better for such readers to be enticed, or even as it were compelled, toward a full reading by the hope of obtaining some extraordinary* **Secret.**

...**piodorus**, <note>This continues the name from the previous page.</note> whom they praise as an explainer <note>original: "enucleatorem" — literally one who removes the pit from a fruit; a detailed commentator who clarifies complex ideas.</note> of **Democritus**; **Pliny** cites certain of his writings as those of a Philosopher. From **Plato**, he explained the *Phaedo*, the *Philebus*, the *Gorgias*, and the *Alcibiades*. These books may be seen in Greek manuscript libraries.

There is also a certain theologian named **Olympiodorus**, whose highly learned **Scholia** <term>Scholia <gloss>Ancient grammatical or explanatory notes written in the margins of a text by a teacher or scholar.</gloss></term> on *Ecclesiastes* are extant. *There is also mention made, among the Greek Alchemists, of **Blemmydes**, or **Blemmida**, concerning **Chrysopoeia** <term>Chrysopoeia <gloss>The alchemical process of "gold-making," or the transmutation of base metals into gold.</gloss></term>. *Furthermore, small Greek books by **Zosimus** are extant, concerning the **Sacred Art**, and concerning the composition of **Waters** <note>In an alchemical context, "waters" (*aquae*) refers to transformative liquid solutions, acids, or elixirs used to treat metals.</note> for **Chrysopoeia**; and also, concerning **Instruments and Furnaces**. **Suidas** <note>Referring to the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia.</note> calls a certain **Zosimus** an Alexandrian Philosopher, and states that he published his **Chymeutica** <note>Writings on chemistry/alchemy.</note>—or **Chiroemata** <note>original: "Chiroemata" — literally "handiworks" or "manual operations," referring to practical laboratory recipes.</note>—dedicated to his sister **Theosebeia** in twenty-eight books, arranged in alphabetical order, as well as a **Life of Plato**.*

*Finally, a manuscript book by **Isaac the Monk** is found, titled **The Method of Silver** <note>original: "τοῦ ἀργύρου" (*tou argyrou*)</note>, as well as his work on **Geodesy**.* <term>Geodesy <gloss>The science of measuring the earth; here likely referring to Isaac Argyros's mathematical and astronomical treatises.</gloss></term>

*Whether they believe this was done out of envy <note>The author suggests some believed the ancients kept the art secret to prevent others from gaining power.</note>, or rather, through a certain ignorance. *These include Greeks, of course, as well as Arabs, Latins, and Jews; indeed, even those who have written anything about this Art in the common and popular tongue <note>The "vulgar" or vernacular languages of the people, as opposed to the scholarly Latin or Greek.</note>. # PREFACE.

*Thus it will come to pass that, from the arrangement of **Furnaces for the Stone** <note>original: "Furnorum Lapidis" — specifically furnaces designed for the "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, just as many methods for preparing it will be proven as there are furnaces established for that purpose—even though some people believe that a great many different methods are proposed by various authors. In the same way, from the arrangement for **Medicine**, you may extract as many Medicines from source materials <note>original: "corporibus" — literally "bodies," referring to the raw mineral or vegetable matter being processed.</note> as there are Furnaces designated for them; specifically, one distinct medicine from each individual furnace. And, because all these operations occur at the same time, the experiments also reveal their results simultaneously. Otherwise, if one were to test each procedure individually, it would scarcely be accomplished in many years.*

*As for the other matters—the regulation of **Fire**, and the **Instruments** and **vessels** <term>vasa: the specialized glassware and ceramic containers like retorts or crucibles used in distillation.</term> which are absolutely necessary for these tasks—it is better to learn these by observation and practical experience than from books or written rules. Some people also save on costs by this method: they have learned how to clean and harden vessels that have been used for one substance so that they can be repurposed for others.*

*One final point, which I should by no means over—*

-># MEMORABLE THINGS #<-

## The Author Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational works on alchemy, magic, and philosophy were attributed.</note>

The authors of this account are Heliodorus, Plutarch, Aelian, Suidas, Pliny, and others <note>These are prominent Greek and Roman scholars and encyclopedists whose works were foundational to Renaissance natural history.</note>. However, I must warn the Reader here that authors are indeed quite in disagreement regarding the identification of this bird. # MEMORABLE THINGS

*...you will find such things as are being stored. While they are still closed and silent, pluck them and store them in small, pitched jars* <term>laguncula</term> <note>original: "lagunculis." Small flasks or jars, often coated with pitch (resin) to make them airtight, used for medicine or perfumes.</note>, *and seal them diligently so that no air can enter. When necessity requires their use, release the lid and expose them to the Sun or the vapor of warm water so that they may open.*

<margin>14</margin> *You will restrain blood dripping uncontrollably from the nostrils if you write these words on the middle of the forehead of the person suffering the hemorrhage* <term>haemorrhagia</term> *using that very same blood: **It is finished**.* <note>original: "Consummatum est." These are the final words of Christ on the Cross (John 19:30). In the early modern period, scriptural phrases were frequently used as "charms" in folk medicine, believed to have inherent power to stop bleeding or heal wounds.</note> *This is a thing proven by many. One might also add here, though it is a side matter* <note>original Greek: "πάρεργον" (parergon). An incidental point or minor addition.</note>, *that borage* <term>borrago</term> <note>original: "borrago." *Borago officinalis*, a herb with blue flowers traditionally used to treat melancholy and lift the spirits.</note> *added to wine encourages cheerfulness. This is why grammarians think borage is named as if it were "heart-bringer."* <note>original: "corago." A folk etymology combining the Latin "cor" (heart) and "ago" (to lead/bring/act). This reflects the belief that the plant "acts upon the heart."</note> *As the saying goes: **Borage says, I always bring joys.**.* <note>original: "Dicit borrago, gaudia semper ago." A popular medieval mnemonic rhyme used by herbalists.</note> *But these are trivial things.*

### 2
The priests of the ancient religion—those ministers of demons—in order to grow wealthy under the guise of religion, used to pretend that the gods tormented men with diseases. Epilepsy was counted among these, and for that reason it was called the **sacred disease** <term>sacred disease: (Latin: sacer morbus) an ancient name for epilepsy, based on the belief that it was caused by divine or supernatural intervention rather than physical causes.</term>. The authority for this is **Hippocrates** <note>original: Hippocr.; Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), the Greek physician traditionally regarded as the father of medicine.</note> in his book *On the Sacred Disease* and *On the Diseases of Virgins*. To this is added **Galen** <note>original: Galen.; Claudius Galenus (129 – c. 216 AD), a Greek physician and philosopher whose works formed the basis of medical knowledge for over a millennium.</note> in his book of *Prognostics*, as noted by **Johannes Langius** <note>original: Ioannes Langius; Johann Lange (1485–1565), a German physician who published influential medical letters.</note>.

<margin>13</margin>
*Aganice, as Plutarch relates, was the daughter of Hegetor of Thessaly. She was highly skilled in the eclipses* <note>original: *siderum defectus*; literally "failings of the stars"</note> *of the heavenly bodies that occur during full moons. Being well-aware of the time when the Moon would be clouded by the shadow of the Earth’s obstruction, she would predict these events to gullible women as a prophecy of the future. This happens much to the wonder of the spectators, who [witness] fire [produced] from water... <note>original catchword: "exci-," likely for "excitari" (to be stirred up or produced).</note>

...written on a tablet. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note>, following the testimony of **Mutianus** <note>Gaius Licinius Mucianus, a Roman general and writer who was consul three times.</note>, left this as a witnessed fact, as did **Plutarch** <note>A famous Greek philosopher and biographer.</note>.

<margin>36</margin> The **North wind** <note>original: "aquilo"</note>, if it rises in the dead of night or at twilight, soon vanishes and abandons its post. For this reason, experienced sailors trust it very little and do not begin a voyage unless it has lasted for three days. The **South wind** <note>original: "auster"</note>, on the other hand, supports the sailors' hope that it will be long-lasting if it rises at the break of the first day. The Greeks confirm this with a proverb: *The South wind on the first day, the North wind on the third* <note>original Greek: "νότος πρῶτος Βορέας τρίτος." This suggests the South wind is reliable from its start, while the North wind only becomes steady after three days.</note>.

<margin>37</margin> The skin from the right heel of a **vulture**, when applied to the right foot of those suffering from **gout** <note>original: "podagra," a painful form of inflammatory arthritis.</note>, and the left skin to the left foot, is said to mitigate and soothe the pains. It will not be absurd to add to these facts what was revealed by a certain divine oracle: that the root of the **dog-rose** <note>original: "cynosrhodi," from the Greek for "dog rose."</note>, which the common people call **sweetbrier** <note>original: "esglantierum," a Latinized form of the Old French/Middle English term for the eglantine rose.</note>, is a unique and singular remedy against the bite of a **rabid dog**—unless you wish to renounce the authority of both **Pliny** and **Galen** <note>A Greek physician whose work dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note>.

<margin>41</margin> Gold, unlike other metals, is not darkened, nor is it covered with soot; instead, it shines and is even made <term>swollen</term> <note>original: "turgidum." <margin>45</margin> *The people of India and Hyrcania <note>Hyrcania was an ancient region located southeast of the Caspian Sea, in modern-day Iran and Turkmenistan.</note> say that the tiger is an animal of tremendous swiftness. Though I did not receive this information for free, I present it to you freely, as I do with many other things.

From this, let husbands learn to be wary of their pregnant wives while they labor under this kind of craving and "pica" <note>a condition where a person craves substances with no nutritional value</note>, or if you prefer, a depraved appetite.*

# CENTURY VIII.

*A matter sought by many, and especially useful and necessary for those who ride on horseback.*

<margin>69</margin> *A **gold plate** <note>original: "Lamina auri"</note> worn over the **cranial suture** <note>the joints between the bones of the skull</note> strengthens the brain. The same, hung over the region of the **heart**, cures its palpitations and increases joy. Placed over the **kidneys**, it strengthens them, cools them, and soothes **nephritic pains** <note>original: "nephriticos"; pains caused by kidney stones or renal disease</note>. But for these purposes, I would prefer it to be manufactured and struck from the purest gold while the **Sun is in Leo** <note>an astrological placement associated with the heart, vitality, and the metal gold</note>, and with **Jupiter** in a favorable aspect with the **Moon**, as we have shown before. Taken from **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note>, **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>, and **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a medieval scholar known for his works on nature</note>.*

<margin>70</margin> *To ensure that a **well** <note>original: "puteus"</note> will have **perennial water** <note>original: "perennitatis fidem"; literally 'the faith of eternity', meaning it will not run dry</note>, it should be dug when the **Sun** occupies the final degrees of **Virgo**, before the **autumnal equinox**. For at that time, the strength of well-water and springs is tested; since, after the long drought of summer, the earth lacks rainwater. These are the teachings of **architects**.*

To these observations I add—even if it is a **secondary matter** <note>original Greek: "πάρεργον" (parergon); a digression or side-note</note>—that the more spirited a horse is, the deeper it plunges its nostrils into the water while drinking, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note>. Additionally, to protect against **hail**, an owl with its feathers and wings spread wide is usefully nailed up, or iron tools are anointed with bear fat, as **Palladius** <note>a 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture</note> relates. I say this practice should be understood as applying to the pruning of trees and vines.

<margin>79</margin> For the **diseases of cattle**, **native sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur vivum"; naturally occurring sulfur not yet processed by fire</note>, **wild garlic**, and a boiled egg are recommended.

...[blight']s harm is turned away from them, as **Apuleius** <note>likely referring to pseudo-Apuleius, the name associated with a popular Late Antique herbal, or Apuleius of Madaura</note> wrote, citing **Berytius** <note>Anatolius of Beirut, a 4th-century writer on agriculture whose work was preserved in the *Geoponica*</note> in the *Geoponica* <note>a 20-volume Byzantine collection of agricultural lore and practices</note>.

<margin>§ 7</margin> The **radish** <note>original: *Raphanus*</note> is more pleasant once the leaves have been removed, just as the **turnip** <note>original: *rapum*</note> is. To prevent fleas <note>likely "garden fleas" or beetles</note> or small pests that grow upon it from doing harm, **Theophrastus** <note>a Greek philosopher and the "father of botany," active in the 4th century BCE</note> commanded that **bitter vetch** <note>original: *ervum*; a grain legume used as fodder</note> be sown among them. He also reports that the same radish is an enemy to grapevines. For if it is planted in their vicinity, they shrink away <note>an example of botanical "antipathy" where plants were believed to physically recoil from one another</note>, as we have taught elsewhere.

<margin>§ 8</margin> The **diamond** <note>original: *Adamas*</note> is so much at odds with the **lodestone** <note>original: *magnete*; a naturally magnetized mineral</note>, especially the *Indian* variety, that when placed near it—or, according to **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13-century scholar who wrote extensively on minerals</note>, placed underneath or even on top of it, in the opinion of some—it does not allow iron to be drawn or seized by the magnet; or if the magnet has already gripped the iron, the diamond takes it away. By this proof, true diamonds can be distinguished from the counterfeits, which are many today. But modern experience denies this **antipathy** <note>original: *ἀντιπάθειαν*; a natural repulsion or "hatred" between two objects</note>, unless those diamonds are entirely false, as we shall discuss a little more fully below.

# CENTURY VIII

<margin>86</margin>
In no other animal will you find a work of lust equal to that of the **partridge** <note>original: *perdice*</note>. For if the females stand opposite the males, they become pregnant from the wind blowing from the males toward them. Furthermore, they gape with their tongues sticking out and pant during that time, and they conceive by the breath of the males sniffing them; often, the conception occurs merely by hearing the male's voice, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), whose *Natural History* is the source of many such wonders of the natural world</note>.

<margin>89</margin>
If **roosters** <note>original: *gallinacei*</note> have tasted the flower of the grape in their food, they will not touch the grapes thereafter. There are some who attribute this effect to **wild dropwort** <note>original: *oenanthen syluestrem*; likely *Oenanthe pimpinelloides*, though in ancient texts it often referred to the flowers of the wild vine</note>; which, when cooked into their food and thrown to them, creates a distaste for seeking out grapes. To these I will add that there is such enmity between **cabbage** <note>original: *brassicæ*</note> and the **vine** <note>original: *vitæ*</note> that they refuse to be planted near each other, according to **Fracastorius** <note>Girolamo Fracastoro (c. 1476–1553), an Italian physician and scholar famous for his works on contagion and astronomy</note>.

<margin>91</margin>
Where any hairy or wool-bearing animal, or even a human being, swarms with worms because of a wound received or for any other reason: if you take some of its hair or wool and, before sunrise, hide it under the bark of that tree which is commonly called the **Aspen** <note>original: *Tremblam*; likely a Latinization of the French *tremble*, referring to the quaking aspen or *Populus tremula*</note>

# OF REMARKABLE THINGS

<margin>95</margin> In **vultures**, the nature of conception is unique and differs from all other creatures. For as **St. Ambrose** <note>original: *D. Ambrosius*; a 4th-century Bishop and Church Father who often used natural history to illustrate theological points</note> noted, they enjoy no intercourse and conceive without the seed of a male, but instead bring forth young without union. On this basis, he writes that all vultures are female, according to the observations of the **Egyptians**. Following these accounts, he claims they are made pregnant by the **East Wind** <term>Euro: the wind blowing from the east</term>, or when the **North Wind** <term>Borea: the cold north wind</term> blows; just as among **Spanish mares**, it is said they are impregnated when the **West Wind** <term>zephyro: the gentle west wind, often associated with spring and fertility</term> blows. Although **Aristotle** <note>original: *Aristoteles*; the Greek philosopher whose works on biology remained authoritative for centuries</note> testifies that vultures fly with their faces stretched toward the **South Wind** <term>austrum: the warm wind from the south</term>, and in this way become pregnant.

<margin>96</margin> **Radishes** <note>original: *Raphani*; likely referring to the large, pungent radishes used in early modern pharmacology</note>, when thrown into or buried within heaps of salt and salt-works, cause the entire mass to melt and dissolve into a watery brine. Because of this property, many conclude that against the **stone** <term>calculum: hardened mineral deposits in the bladder or kidneys</term> and sandy **growths** <term>tophos: stony concretions or deposits formed within the body</term> that have hardened in the body, one should use the water squeezed from the skins—or from the whole body of the radishes. This is taken with white wine and the powder of **turpentine** <term>terebinthinæ: a resin from the terebinth tree, used here in a charred or powdered form</term> obtained from burning...

<margin>64</margin> **Bodies struck by lightning** remain uncorrupted <note>In this context, "incorrupta" means they do not decay or rot like normal organic matter</note>. # TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED AND ILLUSTRIOUS SEQUAN,
<note>The "Sequani" were a people from the Franche-Comté region of eastern France; this dedication is likely addressed to a high-ranking official from that province.</note>

### DOMENICO PIZIMEN-
### TI *of Vibo Valentia, an Italian.*
<note>Vibo Valentia is a city in Calabria, southern Italy.</note>

I observe in these times of ours that very many people claim the name of philosopher for themselves without any right to it. In my judgment, they should by no means be counted among the number of philosophers in reality; instead, they should be cast far and wide out of that true family. For since they spend so little time in the study of wisdom, they are forced to overlook the knowledge of those matters which—unless my mind deceives me—belong to the most excellent part of philosophy. Furthermore, because they waste their entire lives in the controversy over that "prime matter" <term>materia prima: in Aristotelian philosophy, the most basic, formless substance that has the potential to become any physical thing</term> which eludes our sight, and are perpetually occupied in disputes over "form" <term>forma: the organizing principle or essence that gives matter its specific identity</term> and "privation" <term>privatio: the absence or lack of a specific form in a subject</term>, they par-

<summary>In this dedication, Domenico Pizimenti criticizes contemporary scholars who call themselves philosophers but waste their time on abstract Aristotelian disputes rather than pursuing true wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Domenico Pizimenti, philosophy, Aristotelianism, materia prima, form and privation, 16th century scholarship</keywords>

--- Page 548 ---
<meta>The catchword "ticula" from the previous page completes the word "particularium" (particular things). Pizimenti is continuing his critique of "philosophers" who focus only on abstract logic while ignoring the physical study of nature and its secrets.</meta>

...particular matters, and are entirely deprived of the knowledge of wonderful things. Thus it happens that, besides the examination of animals—which are divided into three groups—they shamefully lack an understanding of botany and metallurgy, in which the knowledge of medicine most especially lies hidden. It would be a long task if I wished to recount how much practical benefit is derived from these two subjects. But perhaps I will speak of these things at another time when more leisure is granted. 

For this reason, I will also pass over the fact that Faunus <note>original: "Phaunum"</note>, the son of Picus and grandson of Jove—whom they called Mercury after the name of the planet <note>original: "syderis," literally "star" or "heavenly body"</note>—discovered the metals of gold, silver, and iron. He passed the method for preparing these to the Hesperians <note>A poetic term for the people of the West, usually referring to those in Italy or Spain</note>, and for that reason he received the title "Giver of Riches" from the local inhabitants.

...[ex]plained <note>The Latin text begins with "plicârunt," the conclusion of "explicârunt" (have explained)</note>, I will resolve it in a few words and judge from my own perception: I believe it is nothing else but bodies turned into spirits, joined with their partner in a stable marriage within warm bridal chambers, to procreate golden <note>original: "flavos," often used to describe the "gold" stage or *rubedo*</note> and white <note>original: "candentes," referring to the "silver" stage or *albedo*</note> offspring. ...you shall dye, either copper, or **electrum** <term>electrum: a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver</term>. *Nature rejoices in nature.* I say, whiten **Cyprian copper** <note>original: "Cypriā"</note>, **cadmia** <term>cadmia: a zinc-rich mineral or furnace deposit used in making brass</term>, and **zonites** <note>original: "Zonytem," a poorly defined mineral, likely an earthy variety of calamine or an alchemical "belted" stone</note>, as is the custom; afterward, make it yellow. Manage **androdamas** <term>androdamas: a legendary stone, literally "tamer of men," often identified as hematite or a hard variety of pyrite</term> with harsh wine, or seawater, or sour brine: these are the things that can break down its nature. **Sy.** Because the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> is preferred to the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>.

<summary>Synesius describes the distillation process used to produce "sulfur water," which is essential for dissolving metals. **Dioscorus:** Is it really to be done in this way, O Synesius?

**Synesius:** Not so, Dioscorus. Rather, these matters were arranged in this manner so that they might exercise the sharpness of our mind and intellect. # Verdigris Formation

Take, therefore, one part of **chrysolite** <term>chrysolite</term><note>original: "chrysolithi"; in ancient alchemy, this often refers to various yellow-green minerals or specifically "gold-stone" used to impart a golden hue.</note>, one part of **magnesia** <term>magnesia</term><note>original: "magnesia"; a general term for various minerals (often manganese or magnesium ores) used in the whitening or "cleansing" of metals.</note>, and three parts of **cinnabar** <term>cinnabar</term><note>original: "cinabrij"; mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral and the primary source of mercury.</note>. Grind them together without any moisture; grind them, indeed, until the substances are joined and mixed together, and no more of the **native sulfur** <term>native sulfur</term><note>original: "sulphuris vivi"; literally "living sulfur," referring to naturally occurring, unrefined sulfur.</note> is visible. For it becomes quite black, like the ink that writers use.

Leave this for three days, and then you shall cast it—place it—into a bath <note>original: "lauacro"; a vessel for washing or a liquid medium used for purification.</note>. Wash it with the liquid that is customarily used to wash equal parts, and you will see the sulfur running through it; you will see how it is prepared and how it possesses an incombustible nature.

He calls **copper pyrites** <term>copper pyrites</term><note>original: "chalchopyritem"; a common brassy-yellow mineral containing copper and iron.</note> "lead," and the **Etesian stone** <term>Etesian stone</term><note>original: "lapidem Etesium"; a stone likely named for its origin or seasonal properties, here identified by the author with chrysolite.</note> "chrysolite." This is called the **Great Purification**.

This is simultaneously called **verdigris formation** <term>verdigris formation</term><note>original: "æruginatio"; the process of creating a green patina, representing the extraction of the "green spirit" of a metal.</note> and **blackening** <term>blackening</term><note>original: "denigratio"; the *nigredo* stage, the first major phase of alchemy characterized by decomposition and the color black.</note>.
